Section 21 NIA Act vis-à-vis Framing of Charges: Resolving the Judicial Conflict

The apparent conflict between the judgments of two different High Courts raises an interesting question of law.

The Allahabad High Court held that an order framing charges is not an interlocutory order and, relying upon the Supreme Court’s judgment in Madhu Limaye v. State of Maharashtra, 1978 AIR 47, concluded that an appeal would lie under Section 21 of the NIA Act. The Delhi High Court, however, has taken a different view. Although the Allahabad High Court took note of the Delhi High Court’s judgment, in my view, the reasoning adopted by the Allahabad High Court does not appear to be good law.

The Delhi High Court rightly held that section 21 provides that an appeal, has to be heard on both questions of law and fact. At the stage of framing charges, the Court does not undertake a meticulous examination or appreciation of evidence; rather, the determination is based on grave suspicion and a prima facie view. Consequently, there is no definitive finding of fact at this stage. If the facts themselves have not been conclusively determined, permitting an appeal on both questions of law and fact would be somewhat incongruous, since the factual foundation remains unsettled. Further the framing of charges doesn't even terminate the proceedings. 

Therefore, the Delhi High Court appears to be correct in holding that Madhu Limaye was concerned with the interpretation of Section 397(2) CrPC and that the meaning of “interlocutory order” adopted therein cannot be mechanically imported into Section 21 of the NIA Act, which operates within a statutory framework. The Allahabad High Court relied upon Asian Resurfacing to hold that an order framing charges is not interlocutory. However, a reading of paragraph 21 of Asian Resurfacing shows that the meaning of “interlocutory order” may vary depending upon the statutory provision under consideration. Asian Resurfacing adopted the test in Madhu Limaye because Section 19(3)(c) of the PCA was pari materia with Section 397(2) CrPC, which is not the case with Section 21 of the NIA Act.


In conclusion, the Delhi High Court’s view appears more persuasive, as the test of an “interlocutory order” under Section 397(2) CrPC cannot be mechanically applied to Section 21 of the NIA Act, which operates under a distinct statutory scheme.
